title: Microsoft Adds $450 Billion in One Day, Smashing U.S. Market Cap Record
excerpt: Shares surged 15.5% after blowout earnings showed Azure cloud growth accelerating and AI investments beginning to pay off, easing Wall Street fears about Big Tech spending.
body:
• Microsoft shares surged 15.5% on Thursday, adding roughly $450 billion in market value — the largest single-day dollar gain by any U.S. company in history.
  • Azure cloud revenue grew 43% in fiscal Q4, with management guiding to 45% constant-currency growth next quarter, well above Wall Street estimates of roughly 41%.
  • The company reassured investors it will remain free-cash-flow positive through fiscal 2027 despite planning $175 billion in capital expenditures for calendar year 2026.
  • At least nine brokerages raised their price targets on the stock, pushing the mean target to $560.90.

A Half-Trillion Dollar Day

Microsoft stock posted its best day in nearly 18 years on Thursday, rocketing 15.5% after quarterly earnings eased Wall Street's deepest fear about the AI boom: that the companies building it would spend themselves into oblivion.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=jNDAxtiH394

The rally added approximately $450 billion to Microsoft's market capitalization, eclipsing Nvidia's previous record one-day gain of $441 billion set in April 2025, according to LSEG data. It was also the software giant's best post-earnings performance on record, per Dow Jones Market Data.

The surge single-handedly lifted broader markets. The Nasdaq Composite climbed 2.8%, the S&P 500 rose 1.7%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 1.2% — with Microsoft alone responsible for roughly 360 of the Dow's 614-point advance, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Azure Growth Surprises to the Upside

The catalyst was a fiscal fourth-quarter report that exceeded expectations across the board. Azure, Microsoft's cloud computing division, posted 43% revenue growth, and management guided to 45% constant-currency growth for the September quarter — well above analyst estimates of roughly 41-42%, according to data from Visible Alpha and FactSet.

"The magnitude of the upside for Azure acceleration came in ahead of even the most bullish expectations."

— Kirk Materne, Analyst, Evercore ISI

Microsoft 365 Copilot, the company's AI assistant suite, surpassed 30 million paid seats, underscoring growing enterprise adoption of its generative AI tools.

D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria called Microsoft "the adult in the room," writing that the results "should not only change the narrative on Microsoft, but also communicate that the AI buildout is in responsible hands."

Spending Without Bleeding Cash

What set Microsoft apart from its Magnificent Seven peers was the balance between aggressive AI investment and financial discipline. The company said its capital expenditure plans remain unchanged — $50 billion for the fiscal first quarter of 2027 and $175 billion for calendar year 2026 — but crucially, management indicated it expects to remain free-cash-flow positive throughout fiscal 2027.

That stands in stark contrast to Meta Platforms, whose shares fell 8% on Thursday after projecting negative free cash flow for the second half of 2026, its first such shortfall since going public in 2012. The divergence crystallized a growing Wall Street divide: investors are willing to fund AI ambition, but only when companies can demonstrate returns.

"The key question was whether it could shift the conversation from how much it is spending on AI to what it is earning from those investments, and the results suggested meaningful progress."

— Jake Behan, Head of Capital Markets, Direxion

Microsoft's free cash flow last quarter totaled $19.6 billion, according to the Wall Street Journal, dwarfing Meta's sub-$1 billion figure.

Context: A Stock in Recovery Mode

The scale of Thursday's move also reflects just how beaten down Microsoft had become. Heading into earnings, the stock had fallen more than 18% in 2026, lagging its Magnificent Seven peers. Negative cash-flow reports from Alphabet and Tesla last week had triggered a broader selloff in AI-linked stocks, adding to pressure on the sector.

At least nine brokerages responded to the earnings by raising their price targets, lifting the mean target to $560.90 — well above Thursday's closing price near $451. TD Cowen analyst Derrick Wood called it a "Goldilocks" report that should "support a sustained rally in shares."

What's Next

The immediate test for markets comes from Apple and Amazon, both of which reported earnings after Thursday's close. Amazon beat expectations and its stock jumped in after-hours trading, while Apple's results were more mixed, according to Barron's.

Longer term, the central question for the AI trade remains unresolved. Goldman Sachs estimates that hyperscalers — Amazon, Oracle, Alphabet, Meta, and Microsoft — are on track to issue roughly $250 billion in debt this year for capital expenditures, a figure projected to balloon to $400 billion in 2027.

"I think there's a recognition that this trend can't go on forever," said Jack Ablin, founding partner at money manager Cresset. "They're going to need to start seeing revenue growth."

For now, Microsoft has bought itself time — and nearly half a trillion dollars in market value — by proving it can spend big on AI without sacrificing the cash flow that investors demand.
nri_angle: Microsoft employs tens of thousands of Indian-origin tech workers and its cloud and AI growth directly impacts Indian IT services firms like Infosys and TCS that are key Azure partners.
